name: Négritude
info: Négritude was a framework of critique and literary theory developed in the 1930s by francophone Black intellectuals, writers and artists in Paris, among them Aimé Césaire, Léopold Sédar Senghor and Léon Damas, to cultivate Black consciousness against colonialism and racism.

facts.where: Paris, where students from France’s colonies and territories met at the Clamart Salon of the Nardal sisters and founded L’Étudiant noir; Martinique, Senegal and French Guiana, the homes of Césaire, Senghor and Damas; Dakar, seat of the Dakar School of art; the wider African diaspora.
facts.period: Forerunners from Anténor Firmin (1885) to the Harlem Renaissance; the Clamart Salon and La Revue du Monde Noir (1931–32); the word négritude in L’Étudiant noir (1935); the anthologies of Damas (1946) and Senghor (1948), with Sartre’s “Black Orpheus”; the Dakar School in Senegal (1960–1974); criticism from the 1960s and a scholarly renaissance in recent years.
facts.figures: Aimé Césaire, Martinican poet, playwright and politician, who coined the word; Léopold Sédar Senghor, poet and first President of Senegal; Léon Damas, French Guianese poet; Abdoulaye Sadji; Paulette and Jane Nardal, whose salon brought the founders together; Jean-Paul Sartre, its interpreter; the painters Papa Ibra Tall, Ben Enwonwu and Wifredo Lam.
facts.outcome: A literature and art of Black consciousness and pride that inspired Afro-Surrealism, Créolité, Antillanité and black is beautiful; its founders sought equality within France rather than independence; criticised from the 1960s as insufficiently militant or defensive.

t: Négritude took nègre, a derogatory French word, and made it a name of empowerment; Aimé Césaire first used the word in its present sense in L’Étudiant noir in 1935.
Its founders, Césaire, Senghor and Damas, rejected colonialism, racism and assimilation, drew on Marxism and Surrealism, and celebrated African history, traditions and beliefs.
Paulette and Jane Nardal, who introduced the founders to the Harlem Renaissance in their Paris salon, were long minimised in its history by the masculinist domination of the movement.
dyk: Wole Soyinka mocked Négritude in a 1960 essay: “the duiker will not paint ‘duiker’ on his beautiful back to proclaim his duikeritude; you’ll know him by his elegant leap.”
ev: Anténor Firmin publishes On the Equality of Human Races, a rebuttal of Arthur de Gobineau
Jane Nardal’s article “Internationalisme noir”, on race consciousness in the African diaspora, lays a philosophical foundation
Paulette Nardal and Leo Sajou start La Revue du Monde Noir, a journal in English and French
Aimé Césaire first uses the word négritude in its present sense, in the third issue of L’Étudiant noir
Léon Damas publishes the anthology Poètes d’expression française 1900–1945
Senghor’s Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache appears with Jean-Paul Sartre’s preface “Black Orpheus”
Wole Soyinka mocks Négritude’s “duikeritude”, and Paulette Nardal complains of the neglect of her and her sister’s part
The Dakar School of art, shaped by Négritude under President Senghor, is active in Senegal

sections.background:
Négritude drew on a long line of Black thought. In 1885 the Haitian anthropologist Anténor Firmin published De l’égalité des races humaines (On the Equality of Human Races) as a rebuttal of Count Arthur de Gobineau’s Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races; Firmin influenced Jean Price-Mars, the initiator of Haitian ethnology and developer of Indigenism. Black intellectuals took pride in Haiti for its slave revolution under Toussaint Louverture in the 1790s, and Césaire spoke of Haiti as the place “where négritude stood up for the first time”. The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s and 1930s, whose writers, among them Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, addressed race relations and double consciousness, was a further influence.

In the 1920s and 1930s young Black students and scholars, mainly from France’s colonies and territories, gathered in Paris. There Paulette Nardal and her sister Jane introduced them to the writers of the Harlem Renaissance, and their Clamart Salon, a tea room patronised by Afro-French intellectuals, became a place where Négritude was debated. Paulette Nardal and the Haitian Dr. Leo Sajou founded La Revue du Monde Noir (1931–32), a literary journal in English and French for African and Caribbean intellectuals in Paris, and Jane Nardal’s 1929 article “Internationalisme noir”, on race consciousness and cultural mixing in the diaspora, is seen as the movement’s philosophical foundation.
sections.aims:
Négritude aimed to raise and cultivate “black consciousness” across Africa and its diaspora. Its intellectuals disavowed colonialism, racism and Eurocentrism, denounced Europe’s alleged inhumanity and rejected Western domination and ideas, while promoting African culture within a framework of persistent Franco-African ties. They insisted that Black people possessed a history and a worthy culture equal to those of others, and they took pride in being Black and celebrated African history, traditions and beliefs; the movement showed a Heideggerian interest in Black people’s “being-in-the-world”. They drew on Marxist political philosophy in the Black radical tradition and wrote in a style borrowed heavily from Surrealism.

Assimilation was rejected: to assimilate into a culture that considered African culture barbaric would have been to accept that view. The name itself made the point. Nègre, like its English counterpart, was a derogatory word, and Césaire deliberately built it into the name of his philosophy, re-imagining it as a form of empowerment, while the suffix -itude allowed him to trope the vocabulary of racist science. Senghor noted that “the term négritude has often been contested as a word before being contested as a concept”. Each of the founders had his own idea of its purpose, but all three shared a sense of revolt against the racism and colonial injustice of their world and their French education.
sections.events:
In Paris Aimé Césaire started the magazine L’Étudiant noir with his fellow students Léopold Senghor and Léon Damas, as well as Gilbert Gratiant, Leonard Sainville, Louis T. Achille, Aristide Maugée and Paulette Nardal. In its third issue, of May–June 1935, Césaire first used the word négritude in its present sense, in his first published work, “Conscience Raciale et Révolution Sociale”, which disavowed assimilation as a strategy of resistance and used nègre as a positive term. Senghor’s first critical theory piece, “What the Black Man Contributes”, followed in 1939.

Two anthologies became pivotal. Damas published Poètes d’expression française 1900–1945 in 1946, with an introduction meant as a manifesto; he saw his message as one for the colonised in general and included poets from Indochina and Madagascar. Senghor followed in 1948 with the Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française, which took the manifesto’s role, and its preface by Jean-Paul Sartre, “Orphée Noir” (“Black Orpheus”), carried Négritude into the wider intellectual conversation. From 1960 to 1974 the Dakar School of art in Senegal, founded under the paternalism of President Senghor, gave the philosophy visual form, with a School of Fine Arts created to shape it. In the 1960s some Black writers began to criticise the movement as insufficiently militant.
sections.people:
Aimé Césaire, poet, playwright and politician from Martinique, discovered the Black community and “rediscovered Africa” as a student in Paris. For him Négritude was the fact of being Black, its acceptance and the appreciation of Black history and culture, the means to a “decolonization of the mind”; he held Western imperialism responsible for Black people’s inferiority complex. Back in Martinique he was elected mayor of Fort de France and a representative in France’s Parliament, and he called for Martinique’s political assimilation through the Departmentalization Law. Léopold Sédar Senghor, poet and later the first President of Senegal, used Négritude to work toward a universal valuation of African people and a modern celebration of African customs and ideas, the most common reading in later years.

Léon Damas, French Guianese poet and member of the National Assembly, forcefully defended “black qualities” and rejected reconciliation with white people. Abdoulaye Sadji was also among its progenitors. Paulette and Jane Nardal ran the salon where the movement took shape, and in 1960 Paulette complained bitterly that the two sisters were not acknowledged. Among the visual artists inspired by the philosophy were Papa Ibra Tall, Ben Enwonwu and Wifredo Lam, who brought their training from Western art schools to its themes.
sections.outcomes:
Négritude gave francophone Black writers a shared language of identity and revolt, and its poets wrote of diasporic experience, self-assertion, home and belonging. Damas named the themes of this “indigenous poetry in French”: poverty, illiteracy, the “exploitation of man by man”, social and political racism, forced labour, and “crimes committed in the name of liberty, of equality, of fraternity”. Its visual artists sought to carry African culture and ideas into Western modernity and to break the biases against African art. Neither Césaire nor Senghor envisaged political independence from France: Senghor hoped for a “seat at the give and take of the [French] table as equals”, though France did in time grant Senegal and its other African colonies independence.

Its reception was divided. In “Black Orpheus” Sartre read Négritude as the opposite of colonial racism in a Hegelian dialectic, an “anti-racist racism” whose final goal was racial unity, and so introduced it to French intellectuals. In the 1960s some Black writers found it insufficiently militant: Keorapetse Kgositsile argued that it rested too much on Blackness as a European aesthetic saw it. The Nigerian writers Chinua Achebe and Wole Soyinka opposed it, believing that a declared pride in race put Black people on the defensive; Soyinka wrote that “a tiger doesn’t proclaim its tigerness; it jumps on its prey.”
sections.legacy:
Négritude inspired many movements across the Afro-Diasporic world, among them Afro-Surrealism, Créolité and Antillanité in the Caribbean and black is beautiful in the United States, and Frantz Fanon often referred to it in his writing. Its history has also been revised. In a letter of February 1960 Senghor admitted that the founders had been in contact with Black Americans in 1929–34 through Paulette Nardal’s salon, and Jane Nardal’s “Internationalisme noir” of 1929 came a decade before Senghor’s first theoretical essay. The part of the two sisters was minimised by the masculinist domination of the movement, and their name belongs beside those of Césaire, Senghor and Damas.

After a long silence a renaissance of Négritude has come from scholars such as Souleymane Bachir Diagne of Columbia University, Donna Jones of the University of California, Berkeley, and Cheikh Thiam of Ohio State University, who continue the work of Abiola Irele (1936–2017). Diagne reads Négritude as a philosophy of art and Jones as a lebensphilosophie, and Thiam’s book is the only book-length study of it as philosophy. The word has lived on beyond the movement: Norman Mailer used it of the boxer George Foreman in The Fight, his account of the “Rumble in the Jungle” of 1974 in Kinshasa, and the rapper Youssoupha named an album Négritude.

summary: Négritude was a framework of critique and literary theory developed in the 1930s by francophone Black intellectuals in Paris, above all Aimé Césaire, Léopold Senghor and Léon Damas, who turned the slur nègre into a name of pride. Rejecting colonialism, racism and assimilation, it celebrated African history and culture in poetry and art and inspired movements across the African diaspora, though critics such as Wole Soyinka found it defensive.
references: Rabaka, Reiland, The Negritude Movement: W.E.B. Du Bois, Leon Damas, Aime Cesaire, Leopold Senghor, Frantz Fanon, and the Evolution of an Insurgent Idea (Lexington Books, 2015)
Sharpley-Whiting, T. Denean, Negritude Women (University of Minnesota Press, 2002)
Wilder, Gary, The French Imperial Nation-State: Negritude & Colonial Humanism Between the Two World Wars (University of Chicago Press, 2005)
Irele, Abiola, “Négritude or black cultural nationalism”, Journal of Modern African Studies 3.3 (1965)
Thiam, Cheikh, Return to the Kingdom of Childhood: Re-envisioning the Legacy and Philosophical Relevance of Negritude (Ohio State University Press, 2014)
notes: Dates: the article says only that Négritude was developed ‘during the 1930s’. Start 1931 (La Revue du Monde Noir, 1931–32; the Clamart Salon and Jane Nardal’s 1929 article come earlier) marked circa; the word dates from 1935. End 1974 (the end of the Dakar School, the last dated phase of the movement itself), marked circa; the article also describes a scholarly ‘renaissance of Négritude’ today, so the editor may prefer end null.
Region given as Sub-Saharan Africa; the movement began in Paris among students from Africa and the Caribbean (Martinique, French Guiana, Senegal), as the where fact says.
Rabaka’s title is copied with the article’s misspellings corrected (‘Aime Cesarie’ → Cesaire, ‘Frants Fanon’ → Frantz Fanon) and the place ‘Lanham, Ml’ dropped; the editor should confirm.

Two Soyinka quotations: the article gives ‘A tiger doesn’t proclaim its tigerness’ (no date) and the duiker line ‘in a 1960 essay for the Horn’; the duiker one is the dyk and the 1960 event, the tiger one is in the outcomes.

The article says the Nardals’ ‘name belongs in that list’ in its own voice; the legacy section says the same. Their role (introducing the Harlem Renaissance, the Clamart Salon, Jane’s 1929 article as ‘the philosophical foundation’) is stated as the article gives it.

Left out: Benjamin Rush’s supposed use of the word (disputed in the article), the ‘thingification’ paragraph (unclear), the Spanish-Caribbean negrismo line, Damas’s second anthology date discrepancy (1946 in the text, ‘1947’ for Poètes d’expression française in the Bibliography: I used the text’s 1946).

Wanted but not in the article: Césaire’s Cahier d’un retour au pays natal by its date (only in the Bibliography as a 1997 edition), Présence Africaine, the 1956 Paris congress of Black writers, Senghor’s years as president.
